posts.description:
What started as a weekend project turned into our first hackathon win!

Last weekend, Mirudhula Anbarasan and I won the Build for India AI Hackathon in Chennai!

It was a great experience building Saajhedar together, taking an idea all the way to a working prototype and getting to celebrate the win! It was genuinely inspiring to see what like-minded people are building.

We built Saajhedar - an AI-powered voice partner for businesses

Here’s what it does:
- Discovers business opportunities: Analyses data from 157,000 shops using OpenStreetMap, Open-Meteo and AI-powered neighbourhood analysis to identify market gaps and estimate footfall.
- Manages shop operations: Through multilingual voice.
- Automates procurement: An AI voice agent that directly calls suppliers

The biggest challenge? Getting everything to work end to end rather than building isolated features. From integrating all the components to the usual last-minute debugging and deployment on Linux, there was never a dull moment!

A big thank you to Om Prakash S for taking the time to mentor us and share some valuable feedback that helped us shape our pitch.

Thanks to Mohammed Amer & Om Nitin Tiwari for hosting us

Huge shoutout to Navaneeth Ganesh for bringing great energy to the event and making the experience so memorable!

A special thanks to Anitha KishoreKumar for her time and insights as one of our judges and our tech panel - Dax Percey Abraham, Bhabani Sankar Prusty

Looking forward to building more!
#BuildForIndia #Hackathon #VoiceAI #AgenticAI #Chennai

Super excited to have placed 3rd at the HBS Tech Club's AI Hackathon this past weekend alongside Yvonne Yan, CFA and Cindy Phuong!

Challenged to build a consumer-focused product with real business potential, we created TripBlend - a "Spotify playlist blend" but for group trip planning.

TripBlend gathers basic parameters (location, dates, budget), and hyper-personalized preferences from social media integrations, to create a trip itinerary that the whole group will love. We also envisioned a monetization model using a virtual credit card, that serves users by making splitting trip expenses super easy.

Check out our prototype here: https://lnkd.in/gGSHm7RM

Huge thank you to the Tech Club at Harvard Business School for hosting, and Lovable & Kalodata for sponsoring this fun day!

posts.description:
I saw probably 20 different variations of “10x hackathon winner” titles in the last week.

I fucking hate hackathons and lose respect for anyone who does them. They aren’t a filter for engineering talent. They show how big you can talk and how much you can overpromise. Did you actually “win,” or did you get 3rd place in the 6th category?

You are trying to create the best-looking product in 48 hours, and that’s a breeding ground for useless vaporware. It’s physically impossible to build a useful hardware project in 48 hours. Are you even capable of working on anything for over a week if you don’t get to pitch or announce it every 5 minutes?

The argument from all the npcs whose only goal in life is recognition is that “hackathons are meant to explore ideas,” but 99% of hackathon projects are abandoned. It’s only about winning, and it’s not even impressive because nobody has heard of any specific hackathon

People with all these hackathon wins and openai anthropic startup school founder ambassador fellowships think they’re the shit, then wonder why they get ghosted after the first interview. When everybody’s primary goal is winning, being a better engineer matters less and less. I’ve seen hundreds of reels of people demoing a stupid Arduino project with a get-rich-quick scheme in mind, and I don’t know a single one of them who has executed it end to end.

We make fun of crypto people because they lack the discipline to work hard and look for a shortcut. Hackathons are the same thing. Nobody wants to do the kind of work that takes several months with no instant payoff, and we’re celebrating this get-rich-quick mentality as ambition.
